claims.text: The target material is a high-melting refractory material with a stable crystalline phase below its melting temperature.
A two-phase coexistence or interface-pinning simulation can replace ab initio molecular-dynamics thermodynamic integration for calculating melting properties.
The proposed simulation directly represents a combined solid-liquid system using an efficient DFT-informed interatomic potential.
The simulation is performed near the expected melting temperature under periodic boundary conditions.
A simulation cell containing both solid and liquid phases permits equilibrium migration of the solid-liquid interface.
The dynamically evolving solid-liquid interface mediates the phase transition.
The evolving interface facilitates direct extraction of latent heat at melting.
The evolving interface facilitates direct extraction of the volume change at melting.
Equilibrium coexistence between solid and liquid phases can be used to infer the melting temperature.
Energy differences or discontinuities between the solid and liquid phases can be used to determine latent heat and enthalpy of fusion.
Entropy of fusion can be derived by dividing the latent heat by the melting temperature.
Volume or density differences between the coexisting phases can be used to determine the volume change at melting.
Direct coexistence calculations bypass expensive stepwise free-energy integration.
The proposed method will predict melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, and volume change at melting accurately.
The predicted melting properties will deviate by less than approximately 10% from full ab initio free-energy integration results.
The proposed method has significantly lower computational cost than full ab initio thermodynamic integration.
The reduced computational cost makes high-throughput melting-property evaluation more feasible.
Accuracy may be reduced if the interatomic potential inadequately represents high-temperature anharmonic effects.
Complex or multistep melting behavior may reduce the reliability of the proposed method.
Quantitative agreement depends on interatomic-potential quality and on the material's high-temperature electronic and vibrational behavior.
